strengths: Well-motivated pivot from sample-level to token-level data selection, with clear identification of length and loss-centric biases in existing influence-based methods (Section 1)
Forward-only design is genuinely attractive for scalability; the asymptotic cost analysis (Section 5, Table 4) is careful and correctly distinguishes warmup vs. scoring costs across baselines

Evaluation covers several axes: in-domain budgeted accuracy (Table 1), low-overlap OOD math selection (Table 2), cross-model/cross-scale transfer with an oracle comparison (Table 3), length-bias analysis (Fig. 3), and task-adaptive source distribution analysis (Fig. 4)
Baselines are relevant and reasonably strong (LESS, TAGCOS, S2L, CLD, RDS, DSIR, BM25), with a shared warmup/selection pipeline to reduce confounds
Hyperparameter sensitivity is examined via a single-factor ablation study (Table 8), and the paper is honest in its limitations section about dependence on the small validation set
weaknesses: The core mechanism is heuristic and its central premise is not directly validated: no analysis shows that the attention-derived saliency actually identifies task-critical tokens or that fingerprints encode task structure; attention-as-importance is contested in the interpretability literature and the paper leans on prior work (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020) without evidence that this particular row/column heuristic is meaningful

Headline gains are modest on the main benchmark: Table 1 shows ~1.2 points over LESS (45.37 vs 44.21) with overlapping standard deviations, and the HELLASWAG improvement is within noise (49.08 vs 49.01); no statistical significance tests are reported, and the abstract's 'up to 9%' is driven by the single OOD GSM8K setting

The claimed orders-of-magnitude speedup is only supported by asymptotic analysis; the appendix explicitly states no wall-clock time or GPU-hours are reported (Appendix F.3), leaving the efficiency claim empirically unverified

Several design choices appear arbitrary and only ablated on one task/model (CSQA, Llama-3.2-1B): equal saliency weights, mean+max pooling, coverage term, penalty lambda, and number of layers; notably the ablation that 'None' penalty underperforms lambda=1.0 (Table 8) is confusing, since lambda=1.0 appears to be no penalty at all, and the distinction is not explained

Only LoRA fine-tuning and a limited task suite (3 multiple-choice benchmarks plus GSM8K) at 1B scale for the main results; generalization to full fine-tuning, larger scorer models, or generative evaluation is not shown

Fingerprints are built per token class from only 5-10 samples, meaning most classes will have very few occurrences and many candidates rely on the embedding-space backoff; the sensitivity of the method to this sparsity and to validation-set noise is not characterized (acknowledged but not analyzed)
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many pipeline details (scoring scope, coverage weight, backoff penalty) that affect results
